transcript.text: Hi, our integrated fridge freezer (behind a kitchen door) - the fridge is around 10 degrees but the freezer seems ok. We had a power cut a week ago, not sure if related. Rented flat, can't really take it out.

A fridge at 10°C is too warm (it should be about 3–5°C), so it's worth sorting quickly. The power cut may well be related. Here's what to check, roughly in order of likelihood.

## Quick checks (5 minutes)

1. Settings reset: Some models with digital controls reset to a default after a power cut. Check the display or dial and make sure the fridge is set to around 4°C (or a middle-to-colder setting on a dial).
2. Door closing properly: Integrated fridges are attached to the cupboard door with sliders or brackets, which can loosen. Check that:
• the appliance door and the cabinet door close fully together
• the rubber seal is clean and not torn
• a sheet of paper closed in the door is gripped firmly all the way round
3. Vents blocked: Make sure food isn't pushed against the back wall or covering any vents, especially near the top where cold air often comes in from the freezer.

## Most likely culprit after a power cut: ice blockage

Many fridge freezers cool the fridge using cold air from the freezer, or have a drain channel at the back of the fridge. During a power cut, ice can melt and then refreeze in the wrong place, blocking the airflow or drain. Signs include:
• ice or frost on the back wall of the fridge
• water pooling at the bottom of the fridge
• a freezer that seems fine but a fridge that's warm (which is your situation)

The fix: a full manual defrost. You can do this without removing the appliance.
1. Move food to a cool box or a friend's fridge.
2. Switch it off at the socket or isolator switch. With integrated units, this is often a switched spur above the worktop.
3. Leave the doors open with towels down for 4–8 hours, ideally overnight, until all ice is gone.
4. Clear the drain hole at the back of the fridge if there is one (a cotton bud or a little warm water usually works).
5. Switch back on and allow about 12–24 hours to settle before reloading fully.

## Measuring the temperature properly

Use a fridge thermometer placed in a glass of water on the middle shelf, and check it after a few hours. Air readings jump around every time the door opens.

## Food safety

Anything kept above about 8°C for more than a few hours is risky, especially:
• raw or cooked meat and fish
• dairy, soft cheese
• cooked leftovers, rice
• ready meals, deli items

If in doubt, throw it out. Hard cheese, butter, condiments, and most fruit and vegetables are generally fine.

## Since you're renting

If the fridge freezer came with the flat, repairs are usually the landlord's responsibility. It's worth messaging them or the letting agent now, in writing, even while you try the steps above. If the defrost doesn't fix it, it could be a fan, thermostat, or sensor fault, which needs an engineer. That shouldn't be at your expense, and they'll handle pulling it out of the housing if needed.

Do you know the make and model? It's usually on a sticker inside the fridge. I can give more specific tips if so.
Thanks, I found the sticker inside the fridge. It's a Hotpoint HMCB 7030 AA. No burning smell and nothing's tripping, if that helps.

Thanks, that helps. No burning smell and nothing tripping makes a basic electrical fault less likely, so it's more likely to be ice, airflow, the thermostat, or (less happily) a refrigerant problem.

## About your model

The Hotpoint HMCB 7030 AA is a built-in 70/30 fridge freezer. I believe it's a static (not frost-free) design with a temperature dial inside the fridge, but check your manual to confirm. You can download it free from the Hotpoint UK website by entering the model number.

## Quick diagnosis

With the fridge running, check these:

1. The dial: Make sure it hasn't been knocked to a low setting. Turn it one step colder and recheck the temperature after 12–24 hours.
2. The back wall of the fridge:
• Thick ice or frost: A manual defrost (as described earlier) is the likely fix.
• Cold, maybe with a thin layer of frost or droplets: This is normal. The problem is more likely the door, seal or airflow.
• Not cold at all, even though you can hear the motor humming: This suggests a sealed-system problem such as low refrigerant. A freezer that's fine with a warm fridge is a classic sign of this. It isn't DIY-fixable and needs an engineer.
3. The compressor (the hum from the bottom back):
• Running nonstop but the fridge stays warm: Possibly low gas or a blockage.
• Barely running or clicking off quickly while the fridge is warm: Possibly a faulty thermostat.

## Checking the temperature (completing my earlier point)

Put a fridge thermometer in a glass of water on the middle shelf and read it after a few hours. This gives a truer reading than air temperature.

## Food safety

The fridge should be at 5°C or below, and 8°C is the legal upper limit for chilled food in shops. At 10°C, I'd throw away anything high-risk that's been in there a while, such as raw or cooked meat, fish, dairy, leftovers and ready meals. Your freezer food should be fine if it's still frozen solid.

## Because you're renting

If the appliance came with the flat, its repair is normally the landlord's responsibility. I'd report it in writing now, with the model number and the temperature you're seeing. You can still try the dial and defrost steps, which are low-risk and might save everyone a callout. But if the back wall stays warm, leave it to the landlord's engineer.

The dial is on 3 out of 5, so I can turn it up one. I can hear it running a lot, it doesn't seem to switch off much. I'm not sure how to tell if the back wall of the fridge is properly cold though, the freezer has a bit of frost on the back but not loads.

Constant running is a useful clue. It means the fridge is trying to cool but not keeping up. That points to one of three things: heat getting in (door or seal), heat not getting out (poor ventilation), or a cooling fault (such as low refrigerant).

## How to check the back wall

In your type of fridge, the cooling element is usually a smooth panel on the back wall inside the fridge compartment.

1. Place your palm flat on it for a few seconds while the fridge is running.
• Healthy: Noticeably cold, often icy to the touch, with droplets or a thin layer of frost forming.
• Partly cold: Only one area (often a strip at the top or one corner) is cold or frosted and the rest is just cool. This is a classic sign of low refrigerant.
• Barely cool: Little colder than the air in the fridge, despite the motor running. This also suggests a sealed-system fault.
• Thick ice: A layer of ice, especially if it's several millimetres or more. It insulates the panel, so defrosting is the fix.
2. Look at the bottom of the panel for a drain channel and small hole. If it's blocked with ice or debris, you may see water pooling.

The light frost in the freezer is fine and normal.

## Other things to check while it's running a lot

• Door seal: Do the paper test all the way round the fridge door. On integrated units, the sliders connecting the cabinet door to the fridge door can work loose and stop it closing fully.
• Ventilation: Built-in fridges need airflow, usually through the plinth (kickboard) grille at the bottom and a gap at the top of the housing. Make sure nothing is blocking these, such as boxes, a bin, or a solid plinth with no vent. Poor ventilation makes the compressor run constantly and cool badly. It's also worse in a warm kitchen.
• The cabinet sides: It's normal for them to feel warm. If they feel very hot, that suggests the unit is overheating or poorly ventilated.

## Next steps

1. Turn the dial to 4 and put a thermometer in a glass of water on the middle shelf.
2. Recheck after 24 hours.
3. If it's still above 5°C, or the back-wall check suggests partial or no cooling, it's likely an engineer job.

## Because you're renting (finishing my earlier point)

If the fridge freezer came with the flat, the landlord is normally responsible for repairing or replacing it. Report it to your landlord or letting agent in writing (email is fine). Mention:

• the model number
• the 10°C reading
• the constant running
• the power cut

Don't arrange or pay for a repair yourself unless they agree first, or you may not get reimbursed. Doing a manual defrost or simple checks like those above is fine. A refrigerant problem isn't something to attempt yourself, as it needs a qualified engineer.

In the meantime, keep high-risk foods (meat, fish, dairy, leftovers) to a minimum or in a cool box, and use the freezer where possible.

The plinth has a vent grille and I can't see anything blocking it. The fridge door closes and the cabinet door moves with it. I'm still not sure what the back wall of the fridge should feel like, and I haven't tried the paper test. I'll turn the dial up to 4 and see what happens.

Turning it to 4 is a sensible next step. Here are some easier ways to judge the back wall, and how to do the paper test.

## Judging the back wall

1. Compare it with the side walls. Put one hand on the back panel and the other on a side wall of the fridge. The back panel should feel distinctly colder, more like an ice pack than a cold drink can. If you can't really tell them apart, that's a warning sign.

2. Look for frost or droplets. In your type of fridge, frost or condensation forms on the back panel while the motor runs and melts when it stops. Since yours is running almost constantly, you'd expect to see:
• Even frost or droplets across most of the panel: Probably cooling properly.
• Frost only on a small patch (often top or one corner): Suggests low refrigerant.
• Completely dry and not very cold: Suggests a cooling fault.
• A thick layer of ice: Defrost needed.

3. Do the water drop test (the clearest one). Dab a few drops of water on the panel with your finger while the motor is running. If they turn to frost or ice within a few minutes, the cooling is working. If they just sit there as water, the panel isn't getting cold enough.

## The paper test

1. Open the fridge door and place a sheet of paper (or a banknote) across the seal.
2. Close the door and gently pull the paper out.
3. You should feel resistance. If it slides out easily, that part of the seal isn't sealing.
4. Repeat at several points all the way round, especially the corners and the hinge side.

The cabinet door moving with the fridge door is good. Occasionally, though, the sliders hold the fridge door slightly open, so the paper test is still worth doing.

## What to do next

1. Turn the dial to 4 and put a thermometer in a glass of water on the middle shelf.
2. Recheck after 12–24 hours.
3. If it's down to 5°C or below: You're probably fine, but keep an eye on it.
4. If it's still above 5–6°C and the back panel fails the drop test or only frosts in patches, it's likely a sealed-system fault. That needs an engineer.

## Tell your landlord now

Because you're renting, I'd let your landlord or letting agent know now rather than waiting. A fridge running constantly at 10°C is a reasonable thing to report. If it came with the flat, the repair is normally their responsibility. Put it in writing (email or text) with the model number and what you've noticed. In the meantime, keep high-risk food like meat, fish, dairy and leftovers in the freezer or eat it quickly.
Ok, I'll try the water drop test and the paper test and turn the dial to 4. Will report back after a day. Should I also message the letting agent now?

Yes, I'd message them now rather than waiting a day.

• It creates a record. Tenants are generally expected to report problems promptly, and a dated message shows you did.
• Repairs take time. If it turns out to be a refrigerant fault, the agent will need to arrange an engineer. Getting in the queue now saves days.
• It's usually the landlord's responsibility. If the fridge freezer came with the flat (check your inventory or tenancy agreement), repairing or replacing it is normally down to the landlord, unless the damage was caused by misuse.
• It covers you if the tests fix nothing. You can simply follow up with your results tomorrow.

## Suggested message

> Hi, I'm reporting a fault with the integrated fridge freezer (Hotpoint HMCB 7030 AA). Since a power cut about a week ago, the fridge has been running at around 10°C, well above the safe level of 5°C or below. The freezer seems fine. The compressor is running almost constantly. I've checked the vents and door alignment, and I'm turning the thermostat up and monitoring the temperature over the next 24 hours. I'll update you with the results, but please could you let me know how you'd like to proceed in case an engineer is needed? Thanks.

## A few tips

• Take photos of the thermometer reading and anything notable, such as frost patterns or a gap found in the paper test. They help the agent or engineer and support your report.
• Keep it in writing (email or the agent's portal) rather than only phoning.
• Stick to basic checks. Adjusting the dial, cleaning seals and defrosting are normal user tasks. Avoid anything that involves removing panels or pulling the unit out.
• Keep high-risk food out of the fridge, or keep it to a minimum, until it's reliably at 5°C or below.

Good luck with the tests. Let me know what you find tomorrow and I can help you interpret the results.
